item.title: 'Vertigo' star Kim Novak plans to become compost after death
item.description: Kim Novak, 93, reveals she's arranged to have her body composted after death so loved ones can plant trees, calling it "a beautiful expression."
item.content:encoded:
Kim Novak's final act comes with a twist even Alfred Hitchcock couldn't have scripted.

The "Vertigo" star has arranged to have her body turned into compost after her death so friends and loved ones can use the resulting soil to plant trees. The 93-year-old, who is the subject of "Kim Novak's Vertigo," a documentary about her life and career, first confirmed her plans to People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA).

Novak, who lives on a ranch in Oregon, told Fox News Digital she made the arrangements "a few years ago."

'CRIMINAL MINDS' STAR MANDY PATINKIN SHARES UNCONVENTIONAL PLAN FOR AFTER HIS DEATH

"The idea is that I get to live after I'm gone through trees," Novak said. "It's an exciting adventure because this is what I want after I pass. I want to keep living. And one thing that I've always been short on is patience. And a tree has to have patience. I will get to continue to express myself and be an observer of life. To me, it's a beautiful thought. It's given me great peace of mind because I'm going to keep growing. So I'm excited about that."

"It sounds funny perhaps, but it isn't really," she said. "I can't imagine being turned into ashes or being put under the ground. Both of those concepts are not too attractive to me."

Novak isn't afraid of death, even if her plans may strike some as unconventional. The lifelong nature lover said her connection to the environment has given her peace about what comes next.

WATCH: ALFRED HITCHCOCKS BLONDES HAD A GREAT DEAL OF SEX, AUTHOR CLAIMS

"Some people may not even be aware that's a choice," Novak said. "And I know some people don't like to talk about death, or think they're going to be turned into ashes or be underground. It sounds awful. But you have a choice. You can decide what comes next."

"For me, this was a beautiful concept, the idea of becoming one with the soil," Novak continued. "And with compost, of course, everything grows so much better than if you didn't have it. It helps with growth. You become part of the process. It's natural, it's real, it's honest, it's pure. And I even get to choose the kind of flowers that are going to be part of my compost — forget-me-nots."

Although human composting is legal in Oregon, Novak has arranged for her remains to be transported to an Earth Funeral facility in Washington state to undergo the process, known as natural organic reduction.

"I’m in Oregon, so it's not that big a deal," Novak said.

"However, they’re going to have to pack me in ice in order to make it all the way to this place," she said with a laugh.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Novak acknowledged that additional options may now be available since she made her arrangements years ago.

"I'm having all of my compost, once it's done, delivered to friends and family, a bit of it," she said. "I have instructions for all of them to plant a tree or a shrub, but preferably a tree, because I look forward to keeping growing. That's what it's all about for me. I want to keep growing. This is a beautiful expression of life continuing after death."

When Novak began planning her final sendoff, she knew she didn't want to be buried or cremated. She began exploring other options.

"Here in Oregon, there was one place where I could have had a tree planted over me," she said. "However, it was only one tree. I'd like to be many trees."

According to The Associated Press, Novak was the world's top box-office star from 1958 to 1960. The outlet reported that she stepped away from Hollywood in 1966 to pursue a private life devoted to painting.

"Leaving Hollywood taught me that how I live my life matters," she said. "When I left, what mattered the most was being out in nature. I’ve always wanted to be close to nature and live a natural life. Painting has allowed me to continue expressing myself while out in nature. And every day of my life, I’m painting. I can’t wait to wake up each day and start working on a new painting. Sometimes, I’ll stick with a painting for months just because I haven’t fully figured out what I want to express. It’s been a wonderful way to live a life of expression."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"Films were wonderful too," she said. "It’s just all the other stuff that went with it that wasn’t very appealing. But playing a character, becoming one with another person, that always gave me joy. When I look back at my life, I remember all the wonderful opportunities I was given to become a different, beautiful character. But even then, I was drawing too. I used to always draw the characters I was playing in my script. Every time I’d find some new feeling about my character, I would draw it and paint it."

Novak's film credits include Otto Preminger's "The Man with the Golden Arm," Joshua Logan's "Picnic," "Pal Joey" and "Bell, Book and Candle." Today, she continues to pursue painting away from Hollywood. But Novak believes her story won't end with her death.

"I made my decision because I want to do something good for the environment, and others can too," she said. "After we're gone, the Earth is still here, and we need to protect it. Life goes on when we're no longer here. And in some ways, this doesn't make you feel like you're dying. You're continuing to live on becoming part of the environment. It's something beautiful to look forward to, not dread."

"I don't want to be forgotten," she said. "I want to be remembered not just for films, but for what it made me into, what it turned me into. All the ways I transformed in life, I got to express myself in my art. And I'll continue to express myself."

’Kim Novak’s Vertigo’ is now available to stream or purchase on digital platforms.

item.title: Hochul faces revolt from unlikely New Yorkers as Democrats deliver scathing verdict on their party
item.description: Former Democratic Bronx Assemblyman Stephen Kaufman accuses his own party of being overtaken by socialists while rallying for Bruce Blakeman.
item.content:encoded:
BRONX, N.Y. – Republican New York gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman is courting disaffected Democrats as he seeks to unseat Gov. Kathy Hochul, betting that frustration over affordability, crime and the party's leftward shift could help him make inroads with traditionally Democratic voters.

"They're not Democrats. They're socialists and communists," former Democratic Bronx Assemblyman Stephen Kaufman told Fox News Digital. "They're just not Democrats, they're not moderates."

Kaufman delivered the blistering criticism while rallying alongside Blakeman at the Crosstown Diner in the Bronx, where several voters expressed similar frustrations with Democratic leadership and said they were backing the Republican candidate.

"Every time I go out and meet the people, another Democrat comes up to me and says, 'Bruce, I'm a lifelong Democrat. I've never voted Republican in my life. We're voting for you,'" Blakeman told Fox News Digital.

NY SOCIALIST SURGE COULD PUSH DEM VOTERS TO DEFECT, GOP GOVERNOR CANDIDATE PREDICTS

Kaufman accused the Democratic Socialists of America of gaining increasing influence over the party, warning that Democrats are "rapidly becoming a house of hatred" that no longer welcomes moderate voices.

Several Bronx voters who spoke with Fox News Digital echoed those concerns, pointing to rising costs, public safety and the Democratic Party's increasingly progressive direction as reasons they feel politically abandoned.

"It's not your Democratic Party anymore. It's not your grandfather's Democratic Party. It's become the Democratic Socialist, a.k.a. Communist Party," Lisa, a resident of the Bronx's Throggs Neck neighborhood, said.

"The socialists here literally said we’re land-hoarding if we only have a single-family home or a four-family home and that we were a problem… Kathy was all in support and quiet about it. She didn’t defend the homeowners," another man from the Bronx added.

BRUCE BLAKEMAN HAMMERS DEM GOV HOCHUL, MAMDANI OVER SUBWAY SAFETY DURING NYC CAMPAIGN RIDE

One registered Democrat said the party's failure to address the needs of working families was driving his political decisions.

"I'm a registered Democrat. Ask me if I vote that way," he said. "I vote to what affects me, my community, the people I live with. I vote who's going to help the middle class."

SHOCK POLL: POWERFUL BLUE STATE GOV'S LEAD SHRINKS TO SINGLE DIGITS WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION

Blakeman argued that growing frustration with Hochul's leadership has created an opening for Republicans in a state long dominated by Democrats.

"Kathy Hochul has raised taxes. She's raised utility rates 48 times. Programs like cashless bail make it easier for criminals to operate in our neighborhoods. So now I have the evidences. I have her report card and it's straight F's," said Blakeman.

Kaufman said that Hochul has embraced and catered towards the further left of her party.

THE IRAN WAR DIDN'T MAKE YOUR HEATING BILL THIS HIGH. BLUE-STATE ENERGY POLICY DID

"The electricity rates have skyrocketed. She's had 42 increases over time. She wouldn't permit building of gas lines. She's closed utility plants. All she does is move harder and harder to the left. Which don't represent people in this neighborhood," he said.

"Every time she has a problem, she goes crying to the hard left. She's totally controlled by them," Kaufman added.

Blakeman, meanwhile, told Fox News Digital he would take the opposite approach, pledging to cut taxes and utility bills while making communities safer.

"I will cut taxes. I will cut utility bills. And I will make for safer communities just like I did in my own county as county executive," Blakeman said.

Blakeman pointed to his record as Nassau County executive, saying he has "not raised taxes a penny in five years" and has instead cut taxes by $150 million.

"I’ll take my record, compare it to hers," he said, arguing he would "cut their taxes, cut the utility bills and make safer communities."

The socialist wing of the Democratic Party has moved from the margins to positions of real political power, particularly in New York, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani became mayor and DSA-backed candidates went on to topple Democratic incumbents in congressional primaries.

The movement has also scored victories beyond New York, with DSA-backed Melat Kiros defeating longtime Democratic Rep. Diana DeGette in Colorado and self-described democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George capturing the Democratic mayoral nomination in Washington, D.C.

Fox News Digital reached out to Hochul's office for comment.

item.title: America's little-known castles, displaying 'raw power,' are hiding in plain sight
item.description: Author and historian Dan Jones traces 3,000 years of fortifications in "Castles," from Fort Sumter and Fort Pulaski to the Tower of London's gruesome dark history.
item.content:encoded:
When most Americans think of castles, they likely picture medieval fortresses towering over European hills. 

Yet the history of these imposing structures is much closer to home than many might realize.

Speaking to Fox News Digital from England, historian Dan Jones described his latest book as a 3,000-year journey through human history, from the Sack of Troy to the Nuclear Age, as it explores the broader history of castles and fortifications.

DIVERS UNCOVER ANCIENT TREASURES LINKED TO ROMAN GIANT WHO HELPED SHAPE AMERICAN HISTORY

From Iron Age hillforts to classic medieval castles and beyond, "Castles: A Fortified History of the World," explores fortifications across different eras and regions of the world, including Japan's Himeji Castle and nuclear bunkers built during the Cold War.

Jones examines the role America has played in the broader history of castles, from early fortifications to Civil War-era forts.

"I don't think we can truly understand it without having the American side to the story," said Jones.

One notable example is Fort Sumter in South Carolina, where Confederate forces opened fire on Union troops in April 1861, marking the beginning of the Civil War.

'HIGHLY UNUSUAL' CANNONBALL CACHE FOUND AT CONSTRUCTION SITE IN COASTAL CITY MAY BE WORLD'S FIRST

Jones described Fort Sumter, a coastal fortress built with thick brick walls and artillery defenses, as one of the "descendants of castles" that emerged in America.

Another important moment in the history of castle building, Jones said, came when Union forces attacked Fort Pulaski in Georgia with rifled cannons in 1862.

The fort had been considered nearly impenetrable, but was "blown to bits" within 48 hours, Jones told Fox News Digital.

"Fort Pulaski was just thought to be so strong, you may as well bombard the Rocky Mountains," Jones said.

RARE CANNONBALL EMERGES FROM GROUND AT THE ALAMO, LIKELY UNTOUCHED FOR NEARLY 190 YEARS

"Well, Fort Pulaski was blown to bits in 48 hours, and that was a transformative moment in the whole history of castle building."

Beyond military forts, America is also home to grand, castle-like estates built as displays of wealth and status, including Hearst Castle in California and Gilded Age mansions such as the Biltmore Estate in North Carolina and Belcourt in Newport, Rhode Island.

Asked about the historical significance of America's grand, castle-like estates, Jones said that castles have long served two purposes: providing defense and displaying wealth and power.

In that respect, many of the grand estates built during America's Gilded Age followed the same tradition as the magnificent residences of medieval kings and nobles.

"There's this moment in the Middle Ages where they're combined, but you can see this in America today," Jones said.

"There are colossal fortifications and there are these colossal palatial houses that have always been built by the super wealthy."

He pointed to Disneyland's Sleeping Beauty Castle, built in 1955, as another example of the enduring appeal of castles in the popular imagination.

"These are as much a part of the story of castles as the sort of classic medieval ... stronghold," he said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Even so, the romantic image of castles often contrasts with their darker history.

"The castle can sit on the landscape to intimidate, to terrify, to be a display of raw power," he said.

The history of castles is, of course, also filled with gruesome details, and some of the most famous fortresses served as prisons and sites of torture and execution.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Jones pointed to the Tower of London, where Anne Boleyn was beheaded and Guy Fawkes was tortured following the Gunpowder Plot of 1605.

"I've had dinner in the room in which Guy Fawkes was stretched out on the rack after the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, which is a slightly grisly place to be," Jones told Fox News Digital.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

But castles have also served as zoos, mints and royal residences, Jones noted.

Despite their sometimes dark history, Jones believes the enduring fascination with castles goes beyond what meets the eye.

"Somewhere deep down the story of the castle is the story of building places to protect the things we love," he said.

"That's what connects the whole history of fortification and castle building all the way back to almost the dawn of recorded history."

item.title: Cuba spent decades recruiting American spies. Now Washington is turning the tables on Havana
item.description: Marco Rubio's CIA invitation to Cuban insiders targets Havana's espionage apparatus, pressuring a dictatorship that recruited spies like Ana Belén Montes.
item.content:encoded:
Cuba’s government has spent decades recruiting Americans to betray their country. It objects to Secretary of State Marco Rubio inviting Cubans to cooperate with the CIA. Havana apparently believes espionage should remain a privilege of the dictatorship. The Trump administration is right to disagree.

Rubio is challenging a comfortable assumption in Washington: that Cuba is too broke to matter. A regime unable to keep the lights on can still penetrate a government, compromise an intelligence officer, and help America’s adversaries. Poverty has never disqualified a country from espionage. It can make espionage one of its more valuable exports.

I am an American of Cuban descent who spent more than two decades as a CIA operations officer, including service as chief of station in Latin America. That background leaves me with little patience for the assumption that a failing economy must produce an incompetent security apparatus. Dictatorships allocate resources according to what keeps them in power. Feeding the population and protecting the regime are different priorities. Havana has made its choice repeatedly.

CUBA’S ECONOMIC FREEFALL IS HIDING A NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT JUST MILES FROM FLORIDA: REPORT

The record requires little elaboration. Ana Belén Montes became the Pentagon’s leading Cuba analyst while working for Cuban intelligence. She exposed American intelligence officers and distorted Washington’s understanding of the country she was supposed to assess. Victor Manuel Rocha served as a U.S. ambassador and on the National Security Council while secretly serving Havana. Kendall and Gwendolyn Myers sustained an espionage conspiracy for 30 years.

These were patient investments in access. Cuban intelligence cultivated ideological commitment, steered recruits toward useful positions, and allowed American institutions to supply salaries, credentials, and trust. Montes needed no fortune deposited offshore. Conviction was enough. The most damaging agent may be the respected expert whose colleagues cannot imagine that his judgment belongs to someone else.

ALLEGED CUBAN INFLUENCE OPERATIVE, FAMILY IN FEDERAL CUSTODY AFTER RUBIO REVOKES LEGAL STATUS

The consequences extended beyond stolen documents. Cuba’s Wasp Network penetrated exile organizations and targeted American military facilities. One of its officers was convicted of conspiracy to commit murder in connection with the 1996 destruction of two Brothers to the Rescue aircraft. Four men died, three of them American citizens. Havana’s intelligence operations have carried a human cost that diplomatic euphemisms cannot erase.

Rubio’s invitation puts pressure where it belongs: on the people who keep the regime functioning. An intelligence officer, military official, or party insider may know which Americans Havana has recruited, which foreign services it assists, or who signed an order to arrest a dissident. That knowledge gives him something to offer. Washington should make clear that it is prepared to listen.

FLORIDA ATTORNEY GENERAL JAMES UTHMEIER SECURES STATE ARREST WARRANT FOR RAÚL CASTRO

The invitation also puts a question inside Cuban headquarters that no security chief can comfortably dismiss: Who among us has already answered? Even suspicion can consume time and manpower. Every officer assigned to investigate a colleague is an officer unavailable for another mission. A service accustomed to exploiting American trust should have to spend more effort defending its own.

The work behind that invitation must be exacting. Havana will send fabricators and sources it controls. A volunteer’s hatred of the regime does not establish that his information is true. Verify what he knows, test what he claims, and protect him if he proves reliable. The measure of success is a Cuban agent inside an American institution identified, a threatened source protected, or a Cuban operation stopped.

US SANCTIONS FIVE CUBAN ENTITIES, CASTRO FAMILY MEMBER IN LATEST PRESSURE CAMPAIGN, RUBIO SAYS

The president needs to know who works for Havana inside our institutions, what its partners receive, and where its chain of command is vulnerable. A negotiator who knows what the other side is concealing is harder to deceive. A counterintelligence service that can identify the next Montes before she spends years in place can prevent damage that no prosecution will undo. That is the return on patient intelligence work.

Havana will call cooperation with Washington treason. A dictatorship always finds it convenient to confuse its own survival with the life of the nation. Cubans who expose the officials imprisoning their neighbors or the intelligence networks threatening other countries need no lecture on patriotism from the people responsible. The regime does not own their allegiance merely because it controls their passports.

CUBA'S FOREIGN MINISTER ACCUSES MARCO RUBIO OF LYING TO AMERICANS TO JUSTIFY ACTION AGAINST CUBA

President Donald Trump and Rubio are right to force this choice. Pressure should make service to the regime more costly, while a credible opening gives insiders a reason to leave it. Washington must sustain both long enough to produce results.

The Cuban services have operated on a timetable measured in decades. America cannot answer with an attention span measured in news cycles.

For decades, Havana asked Americans to betray a free country. Washington should welcome Cubans willing to help their country become one.

item.title: NBA star torches fan base after boos rain down after first half: 'They are not welcome anymore'
item.description: Nikola Jokic told Denver Nuggets fans who booed at halftime they are "not welcome anymore" after a dramatic 18-point comeback over the Pelicans.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Nuggets are two games into the regular season and three-time NBA MVP Nikola Jokic is already fed up.

The Nuggets eked out a 141-135 victory over the New Orleans Pelicans on Saturday night. Jokic finished with 35 points, 15 rebounds and 10 assists. It was a pretty average night from Jokic, who is known for putting up that stat line on a nightly basis.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Denver was down 75-57 going into the locker room at halftime. Jokic and the rest of the team heard boos from the fans at the Ball Arena. The dominant center rebuked those who booed after the team came all the way back to win.

"We got booed at our first home game, and I think those fans who booed us, they don't need to come anymore," he said, via ESPN. "If you guys follow us, you know that we never quit and we've come back from much worse situations. So, if they ask me, they are not welcome anymore."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Denver shot 48% from the floor and was 32% from beyond the arc. The Pelicans were able to score 15 points off 12 Denver turnovers.

Nuggets fans have hoped Denver would have avoided an 0-2 start to the season after dropping the first game of the year to the Oklahoma City Thunder.

Denver finished 54-28 last season and third in the Western Conference. However, the team was ousted from the first round of the playoffs in six games thanks to the Minnesota Timberwolves. The Nuggets are riding a streak of four straight years of at least 50 wins but only have one title to show for it.

It’s the best the Nuggets have consistently been in years and fans are hoping that more than one Larry O’Brien Trophy can come home to the Rocky Mountains before the window truly closes.

item.title: NFL overcomes civil unrest, Trump concerns and calls to postpone as Steelers and Saints kick off in Paris
item.description: The NFL kicked off at Stade de France despite Paris protests and calls from Trump to postpone the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints game.
item.content:encoded:
After the wisdom of America's most popular sport was questioned over its insistence to play its first-ever game in France in the wake of a Saturday filled with protests and violence, the NFL kicked off inside Paris's Stade de France on Sunday.

So, we've learned a lesson: The league that played the fabled Ice Bowl in temperatures of minus-13°F, played the Fog Bowl in zero visibility, and played Super Bowl XXIII just days after riots in Miami, has a new a benchmark for playing despite difficult circumstances.

Surrounded by a heavier security presence than perhaps any NFL regular-season game before, the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints kicked off just as the league planned for months at around 3:30 p.m. Paris time (9:30 a.m ET in the United States).

NEARLY 1,000 ARRESTED ACROSS FRANCE AS POLICE FIND POTENTIAL WEAPONS ON PROTESTORS: OFFICIALS

The game is being played in the wake of an exhausting Saturday in which a government estimated 110,000 protesters consisting of students, workers, farmers, socialists, communists, pro-Palestine Muslims, anarchists, Antifa and other radicals took to the streets to march, battle police, and cause civil unrest.

And although that unrest forced the shuttering of Saturday's three official fan events planned by the NFL, Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints, it didn't claim Sunday's game.

Stade de France, approximately nine miles north of the Eiffel Tower, was near capacity at kickoff.

It is unknown if the game has faced any credible security threats prior to kickoff. Emails to the league's security department and the Prefecture de Police de Paris have not been answered by publication time.

And while the teams and players will tell the tale of this game, the story of how it remained as scheduled despite the surrounding violence is an equally compelling and perhaps controversial narrative.

FRANCE'S TOP SOCCER TEAM OBEYS POLICE ORDER TO MOVE SUNDAY MATCH; SAINTS, STEELERS OWNERS MEET WITH MACRON

The NFL is playing this first game in France after calls from pundits, at least one player's wife, and even the President of the United States to postpone or relocate.

Paris Saint-Germaine rescheduled its Saturday match to Monday because of the unrest and that fed the chorus of voices calling for the NFL to do the same.

But when asked by OutKick if it still expected to play the game amid the postponement of the soccer match and the shuttering of its own pregame fan events, the NFL had a one word answer:

"Yes."

The NFL reached that decision even though President Donald Trump admitted he was "worried about it," and went on to admit, "I would've said the NFL could've probably postponed that match, if you want to know the truth."

The NFL faced similar calls to back down throughout the past week.

NFL MONITORS FRANCE STREET VIOLENCE BEFORE SAINTS-STEELERS GAME NEAR PA RIS WITH A MAJOR DECISION LOOMING

But the week was filled with the league officials saying they were moving ahead with the game, with the understanding it had contingencies for doing something else if necessary.

NFL executive vice president for Club Business and International Peter O'Reilly said last week the league was being "vigilant" about the situation in France but still confident the game would go forward.

"We've got confidence in the plans both from an ops and security standpoint," he said.

That confidence was echoed by Commissioner Roger Goodell, who informed reporters that he had been in contact not just with the U.S. Department of State but with Secretary of State Marco Rubio himself.

EXCLUSIVE: SECRETARY OF STATE MARCO RUBIO GIVES NFL COMMISSIONER ROGER GOODELL ASSURANCES ABOUT PLAYING IN FRANCE

Rubio confirmed to OutKick that the U.S. Embassy and France believed the game would "be fine."

The intriguing thing about this game and the NFL's recent misadventure in London, where Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts flew approximately 11 hours roundtrip while battling a blood clot that got worse after the return flight home, is that more players have openly questioned the league's embrace of international games.

Steelers wide receiver DK Metcalf was asked in France if there is a country he would like to play a next international game?

"No, sir," Metcalf said, "because I really don't like traveling outside the U.S. to play football."

item.title: Man admits beating dad to death in picturesque town decades ago after bragging to cops about 'first body'
item.description: Douglas Herlihy admitted to killing his father in a New Hampshire home in 2003. A closet door message and a 2020 boast to police helped crack the case.

A New Hampshire man faces up to 24 years in prison after pleading guilty to killing his father more than 20 years ago.

item.title: Catholic alcohol consumption drops to record low as Americans rethink moderate drinking habits
item.description: Catholic adults now report drinking rates near the levels of Protestants as shifting health views and social habits reshape moderate drinking in America.
item.content:encoded:
A historic shift in American drinking habits shows Catholic alcohol consumption reaching record lows, though scientific experts caution against attributing the drop strictly to religious or cultural changes.

The share of Catholic adults in the United States who report drinking alcohol has fallen to 55%, according to a Gallup report authored by analyst Frank Newport.

That marks a decline from the 2002–2004 period, when 79% of Catholics reported consuming alcoholic beverages. Over that same timeframe, self-reported Protestant drinking rates remained flat at 54%.

HEAVY DRINKING SURGES AMONG AMERICANS IN ONE AGE GROUP AS OTHER GENERATIONS CUT BACK

"Drinking has dropped significantly within both the group of those who have no religious identity and, in particular, among Catholics," Newport wrote in the analysis.

However, experts urged caution when drawing sweeping conclusions from subgroup survey data.

Dr. Joshua Gowin, an associate professor in the Department of Radiology at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus who studies alcohol's effects on the brain, noted that self-reported polling figures can fluctuate based on sampling.

"There's definitely a general pattern of alcohol use decreasing across groups," Gowin told Fox News Digital.

"As far as the subgroups go, it wasn't clear or necessarily compelling to me that one group was showing a broad trend that wasn't reflected in the other groups," he went on. 

BRAD PITT SAYS HE CAN DRINK IN ‘RESTRAINED MANNER’ AFTER 7 SOBER YEARS, BUT EXPERT RAISES RED FLAG

"It seemed like really only one data point showed that effect ... which made me a little skeptical that this is a broader phenomenon versus a single survey sample."

Despite methodological limitations in tracking specific religious subgroups, researchers agree that broader social and health trends are driving a shift in overall drinking habits.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Gallup findings indicate that a majority of Americans now view moderate drinking — defined as one or two drinks per day — as bad for their health.

In the latest polling, 52% of Catholics said moderate alcohol consumption is bad for health, alongside 56% of adults with no religious affiliation and 48% of Protestants.

Gowin noted that this public shift reflects decades of neuroscience and medical research.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Twenty years ago, there was still kind of a push and pull between some benefits of alcohol and then some things that even then we knew were potentially harmful," he said.

"Over time, we've gotten a lot more clarity on the things that are bad for our health ... the balance has just shifted more in favor of the evidence for negative health effects."

Gowin pointed out that large-scale neuroimaging studies now consistently link higher alcohol consumption to reduced brain volume, reinforcing public health warnings.

Researchers also attribute shifting consumption patterns to broader societal changes, including shifts in social behavior and loneliness.

Much of America's alcohol consumption has historically occurred in group settings, and changes in how people gather socially may be influencing drinking habits, they believe.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

At the same time, experts caution that a drop in general social drinking does not mean severe alcohol problems have dissolved.

"One of the things that is a bit of a contradiction ... is that although the overall prevalence among all adults is down for the number of drinkers, there is actually a larger number of alcohol-related deaths in the past few years," Gowin noted.

"It's not like the serious problems have gone away."

item.title: Giant robotic claws will grab dead satellites in space
item.description: ClearSpace UK's robotic spacecraft with giant claws will chase down dead satellites at 17,000 mph, with a 2029 launch from Scotland planned.
item.content:encoded:
Space is getting crowded, and I'm not talking about astronauts. Thousands of pieces of junk are circling Earth at incredible speeds. Some are dead satellites. Others are leftover rocket parts or fragments from past collisions. Any one of them could cause serious trouble if it hits a working spacecraft.

Now Britain has a pretty wild solution. It's developing a robotic spacecraft with giant claws that can grab dead satellites and move them toward a fiery end in Earth's atmosphere. Think of a garbage truck in orbit, except this one has to track down its trash while both objects are traveling thousands of miles per hour.

The UK is putting roughly $81 million behind the project. And if everything goes according to plan, the mission could change how we deal with the growing mess above our heads.

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

WILL A FOUR-ARMED ROBOT REPLACE ASTRONAUTS IN SPACE?

The UK Space Agency has selected aerospace company ClearSpace UK to develop a spacecraft specifically designed to remove dead satellites from orbit. The contract is valued at approximately $81 million. The project is part of Britain's Active Debris Removal mission, known as UK ADR. The spacecraft is targeted for launch in 2029 from SaxaVord Spaceport in Scotland's Shetland Islands.

Its first job will be to remove two defunct UK-registered satellites from low Earth orbit. The government wants both satellites removed by 2032. If successful, the mission would demonstrate that one spacecraft can capture and dispose of multiple dead satellites without being sacrificed after its first cleanup. That could make future operations far more practical, especially as the number of satellites in orbit continues to grow.

Catching a satellite sounds straightforward until you consider what's happening in orbit. Objects in low Earth orbit typically travel at roughly 17,000 mph or faster. Some dead satellites may also tumble, making them difficult to approach safely. That's where ClearSpace's robotic technology comes in. The spacecraft will use a specialized capture system to approach and secure an inactive satellite. First, it must carefully coordinate its movements with the target. Then its robotic capture mechanism will take hold of the object.

Once the satellite is secured, the spacecraft will move it into a lower orbit and release it. Atmospheric drag will eventually pull the abandoned satellite down, causing it to reenter Earth's atmosphere, where it is expected to burn up. The cleanup spacecraft itself is being designed for potential refueling and reuse. That means it could remain in orbit for future work instead of ending its mission after disposing of one satellite. Of course, engineers still have to prove the technology can handle these demanding operations safely.

You might assume there's plenty of room in space for a few broken satellites. Unfortunately, some of the orbital regions where satellites operate are becoming increasingly crowded. According to the European Space Agency's space debris statistics, updated October 14, 2026, approximately 47,140 objects are regularly tracked in Earth's orbit. That figure includes functioning satellites, inactive spacecraft, rocket bodies and debris.

And those are only the objects large enough to track reliably. ESA estimates that millions of smaller pieces also surround Earth. The danger comes from their enormous speeds. A piece of debris measuring just one centimeter can carry enough energy to disable a spacecraft. ESA has also warned that an impact of that size could penetrate the protective shielding of the International Space Station.

Now consider what happens when two large objects collide. They can break apart and produce many additional fragments, each capable of damaging something else. Scientists call this potential chain reaction the Kessler syndrome. If enough collisions occur, certain orbital regions could become extremely hazardous for future missions. ESA's 2026 Space Environment Report warns that active debris removal will be necessary to prevent long-term debris growth driven by collisions.

TRUMP TO TRANSFORM SPACEFLIGHT FROM SPECTACLE TO STATUS QUO TARGETING 3 LAUNCHES PER DAY

The danger extends beyond expensive satellites. Astronauts aboard the International Space Station face risks from debris traveling through orbit. In November 2021, crew members took shelter inside their spacecraft after a Russian anti-satellite weapons test created a dangerous cloud of debris. NASA confirmed that astronauts and cosmonauts closed hatches and sheltered inside docked Dragon and Soyuz spacecraft while teams evaluated the threat.

Fortunately, the station and crew remained safe. The incident demonstrated how quickly debris from a satellite breakup can disrupt operations in orbit. A serious impact could damage critical systems or puncture a spacecraft's pressurized structure. That's why space agencies continuously monitor debris and sometimes adjust spacecraft orbits to avoid potential collisions. Removing larger abandoned satellites could help prevent future collisions that create even more fragments.

Here's another concern that deserves attention. Some space debris eventually returns to Earth, and certain components can survive the intense heat of atmospheric reentry. Most smaller debris burns up. However, larger objects and components made from heat-resistant materials can sometimes reach the ground. As rocket launches increase, researchers are paying closer attention to this danger.

Space environmentalist Ewan Wright, from the University of British Columbia, told Space.com that approximately 124 rocket stages reentered Earth's atmosphere uncontrolled in 2024. He estimated that if that annual level continued for a decade, there would be a 33% probability of at least one person somewhere in the world being killed by falling rocket debris. That estimate describes a cumulative global risk from rocket stages, rather than the danger posed by Britain's two satellite-removal targets.

ESA also reports that the risk of casualties from uncontrolled reentries has increased in recent years, although the overall probability remains low compared with many everyday risks. The takeaway here is that removing debris from orbit requires careful planning. Operators must consider what happens when that material eventually returns to Earth.

Britain's mission could have implications well beyond the two satellites it plans to remove. For years, many satellites were designed primarily to complete their missions and then be retired. Some remain in orbit long after they stop functioning. Now companies are developing spacecraft capable of approaching other satellites and performing tasks that once seemed incredibly difficult.

ClearSpace's mission could help prove that robotic spacecraft can safely capture objects that were never designed for servicing. Its planned refueling capability is particularly interesting. Instead of launching a new cleanup vehicle for every job, operators could eventually service an existing spacecraft and send it after more debris.

That could open the door to a new commercial industry. Satellite operators might eventually pay specialized companies to remove aging equipment or extend the useful lives of working spacecraft. However, the UK mission remains in development. Its long-term commercial potential will depend on whether the technology performs as expected.

You probably don't spend much time thinking about abandoned satellites while checking the weather or following GPS directions. But the technology operating above Earth plays an enormous role in everyday life. Satellites support communication networks, provide navigation signals and deliver information used for weather forecasting. They also help scientists monitor changes on Earth and support emergency response operations.

GPS satellites operate in medium Earth orbit, much higher than the low Earth orbit debris targeted by Britain's mission. Still, the broader effort to keep orbital regions safer helps protect the infrastructure that supports satellite-based services. A collision that disables an important spacecraft could disrupt operations and force companies or government agencies to rely on backup systems. Replacing a damaged satellite can also be expensive.

Britain's robotic cleanup mission won't eliminate the space junk problem overnight. But successfully removing two abandoned satellites could help establish a practical way to deal with dangerous objects already in orbit. And with thousands of additional satellites being launched, finding a reliable way to retire them safely could become increasingly important.

I have to admit, the idea of a spacecraft chasing down dead satellites with giant robotic claws sounds like something Hollywood dreamed up. But I find the technology fascinating, especially when you consider how much we depend on satellites without giving them a second thought. What really caught my attention is the possibility of reusing the cleanup spacecraft. That could make removing space junk a routine service rather than an occasional experiment. Still, I wonder whether we're moving fast enough. With companies launching more satellites every year, cleaning up two abandoned spacecraft feels like a small start. I'd like to see satellite operators take greater responsibility for what they leave behind. After all, we wouldn't tolerate companies abandoning broken equipment on our highways. Why should Earth's orbit be any different?

item.title: Fake Social Security statement email hides a scam
item.description: A fake Social Security statement phishing email uses the SSA logo and a convincing layout, but the sender's domain instantly exposes the scam.
item.content:encoded:
There's something about an email from Social Security that makes you pay attention. After all, we're talking about your retirement benefits and years of earnings. So when a message lands in your inbox saying your statement is ready, clicking to take a look might seem perfectly reasonable. That's exactly what scammers are counting on.

Take a look at this email below that recently landed in an inbox. It looks professional, carries the Social Security Administration (SSA) logo and includes a button to view a statement. However, a closer inspection reveals something the sender probably hoped you wouldn't notice. The message came from an email address with no apparent connection to the federal government.

Even more concerning, the Social Security Administration's Office of the Inspector General warned in February 2026 about a significant increase in fraudulent emails using this same type of trick. Here's how to spot the warning signs in this email and protect yourself before scammers get their hands on your personal information.

Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

FAKE CHATGPT BILLING EMAILS CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN

The message arrives with the subject line "Statement Support Was Posted to Your Account Details Report." The sender appears as "Social Security Administrator," which immediately gives the impression of an official government communication. Inside, the email announces, "Your statement is ready." It goes on to say your 2025 Social Security statement is available and invites you to review your earnings record and benefit estimates online.

There's even a neatly formatted box showing the year as 2025 and the status as "Ready." Below that sits a prominent blue "View statement" button. The message also displays what looks like the official Social Security website address. For someone quickly checking email before work or while getting through a crowded inbox, this could easily pass as a routine government notification.

Here's where the message falls apart. Although the sender's display name says "Social Security Administrator," expanding the sender information reveals an address using the domain loradmiadministraciones.com . That's a major red flag. The address has no apparent relationship to Social Security, and the sender's domain does not end in .gov. Scammers can customize their display names to impersonate government agencies or other trusted organizations.

According to the Social Security Administration, most legitimate SSA emails come from government email addresses. However, the agency does use some authorized outside services, including certain communications from echosign.com and approved marketing firms. That means you should examine the complete sender address and verify any unexpected request independently. Even a familiar-looking sender address can be spoofed.

FAKE PATIENT PORTAL SCAM CAN STEAL YOUR LOGIN AND INFECT YOUR PC

The email encourages the recipient to click "View statement" to access what appears to be a routine financial document. That button is a central concern. A phishing link can redirect you to a fraudulent website designed to steal account credentials or sensitive personal information. Some malicious links can also lead to malware downloads.

We haven't verified the destination behind the button in this particular email. However, the suspicious sender address and resemblance to known SSA phishing campaigns make the message unsafe to trust. The SSA's inspector general has specifically warned about fake statement notifications containing dangerous links. Those links could expose personal information or compromise devices.

One interesting thing about this example is how little pressure it puts on the reader. There's no demand for immediate payment or warning that benefits will disappear within 24 hours. Instead, the message offers something people might genuinely want to see: their Social Security statement.

It also uses the generic greeting "Dear Beneficiary," despite appearing in an inbox associated with a named recipient. That lack of personalization provides another reason to investigate, although generic greetings alone cannot prove an email is fraudulent. The professional appearance does much of the work. The SSA logo and government-style formatting create an impression of credibility. Yet none of those visual elements establishes who actually sent the email.

Yes, and that's what makes this scam particularly convincing. According to the SSA's official guidance, people with a personal my Social Security account generally receive an annual email reminder approximately three months before their birthday. The agency also sends certain notifications about new messages and notices. Scammers take advantage of these legitimate communications by creating messages that resemble official SSA reminders.

Before opening a statement or following instructions in an unexpected email, take a few seconds to investigate the message.

On a computer, click the sender's name or expand the message details to reveal the full email address. On an iPhone or Android phone, tap the sender's name or address to view additional information. The exact method depends on your email app. Look closely at the domain. Watch for unfamiliar company names, extra characters or addresses unrelated to Social Security.

On a computer, hover your mouse over a button or link without clicking. Your browser or email app may display its actual destination. On a phone, some email apps let you touch and hold a link to preview its address. Be careful because certain apps may open or begin loading a preview. When in doubt, skip this step and visit the official SSA website yourself. Remember that a website beginning with HTTPS can still be fraudulent. Encryption alone does not prove that a website belongs to the government.

The most reliable approach is to open a new browser window and visit ssa.gov yourself. You can also contact Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 using the number published on its official website. Avoid using contact details provided in a suspicious email.

You can check your earnings record and estimated retirement benefits without clicking an emailed statement link.

If you don't already have an account, follow the official registration instructions. Creating an account can also help you monitor your Social Security information for unexpected activity.

A convincing email can catch anyone off guard, especially when it concerns retirement benefits or personal financial information. These practical steps can help protect your identity and accounts.

Even when an email looks authentic, use the SSA website independently to access your information. Avoid downloading unsolicited statement attachments or documents that claim to come from the agency.

Use a unique password for your Login.gov or ID.me account and keep multifactor authentication enabled. Also protect the email account associated with your Social Security profile because criminals may target it to reset other passwords.

Strong antivirus software can help identify dangerous websites and block known malware downloads. Keep your operating system, browser and security software updated to protect against newly discovered threats. Never provide your Social Security number or financial account information through an unexpected email link. If someone claims to represent Social Security and requests sensitive details, contact the agency through its official website.

Review your earnings history periodically through your personal SSA account. Look for unfamiliar earnings or changes to account details. If you notice something suspicious, contact Social Security directly for assistance.

Scammers can collect personal details from people-search websites and data brokers to make their messages more convincing. Consider removing your information from these websites or using a reputable data removal service to handle supported requests. Although this won't stop every phishing attempt, it can limit some of the personal details criminals find online. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com

The SSA Office of the Inspector General accepts reports of Social Security impersonation scams at oig.ssa.gov/report/ . Save the suspicious sender address and relevant screenshots. You can also report the message through your email provider's built-in phishing-reporting feature. Once you've preserved the information needed for a report, delete the email.

Your next steps depend on what happened after you clicked. Here's how to respond.

Close the suspicious website immediately. Avoid interacting with additional prompts or downloading files. If the site attempted a download, check your device's Downloads folder without opening the file. Simply visiting a phishing page does not automatically mean your information was stolen. However, keep your browser and operating system updated, and run a security scan with strong antivirus software if you notice anything unusual.

Change the affected password immediately through the legitimate website, preferably using a trusted device. If you reused the password anywhere else, change it on those accounts too. A reputable password manager can help you create strong, unique passwords for each account and alert you to passwords that may have been exposed in a data breach. Next, review account activity and recovery settings. Check for unfamiliar sign-ins or unauthorized changes. Contact Login.gov, ID.me or the affected service through its official support channels if you believe someone accessed your account.

Visit IdentityTheft.gov for a personalized recovery plan. Consider placing a free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. This can help prevent criminals from opening new credit accounts using your information. You should also review your credit reports and monitor financial accounts for unauthorized activity.

Avoid opening the downloaded file if you haven't already. If you ran it, disconnect the affected device from the internet and perform a scan with strong antivirus software. If you suspect malware installed successfully, use a separate trusted device to change sensitive passwords. Consider getting professional assistance before signing back into financial accounts on the affected computer.

Contact your bank or financial institution immediately. Explain what happened and ask about securing your accounts or disputing unauthorized transactions. You should also report the incident to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/ and the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/ . The SSA's inspector general recommends these reporting channels for victims of Social Security impersonation scams. If you experienced financial loss, consider filing a report with local law enforcement.

What concerns me about this particular scam is how routine the email feels. There are no dramatic threats or wild promises. It simply tells you that your Social Security statement is available, something millions of Americans have a legitimate reason to check. And the design is convincing enough that someone could click before thinking twice. I've said it before, and I'll keep saying it: A polished email doesn't tell you anything about who's really behind it. In this example, checking the sender's actual address exposed a serious warning sign immediately. My advice is simple. When an email involves your Social Security information, go directly to the government website and check for yourself. A few extra seconds of caution could save you from a much bigger headache.

item.title: More questions than answers: Arch Manning likes the disrespect, Big 12's disaster and a CFP race in disarray
item.description: No. 2 BYU fell to UCF in double overtime after chaos erupted in regulation, while Texas Tech lost to unranked Cincinnati in a wild Big 12 weekend.
item.content:encoded:
So, turns out 'survival weekend' in college football did not go as planned for a number of teams across the country on Saturday, as for the consecutive weeks the No. 2 ranked team in the sport went down in dramatic fashion.

This time it was No. 2 BYU falling victim to the hangover, losing to UCF in double-overtime that turned into pure chaos over the final few minutes of regulation, after defeating Notre Dame last week.

And, maybe Steve Sarkisian was right this past week in the buildup to the Ole Miss showdown that everyone involved in the talk around Arch Manning, even if warranted, created a monster in the Texas quarterback.

How did Arch feel about the commentary around him this week? He admitted it's a never ending cycle, though he's starting to enjoy the doubters in his 'edgy' era.

"I've been hyped up all my life, the preseason and all this stuff," Manning explained after the win over Ole Miss. "I think I kida like being disregarded kinda now."

ARCH MANNING, TEXAS SURVIVE OLE MISS AFTER ANOTHER SECOND HALF MELTDOWN CREATES ANXIETY IN AUSTIN AFTER REBELS FRENZY COMEBACK

A win over the No. 7 Rebels have put the Longhorns back into the CFP conversation in dramatic fashion, with a statement win over an Ole Miss team who was coming off a bye-week.

It was also the Big 12 Conference that was at the forefront of madness this week, taking a page out of the SEC's playbook after last weekend, while both No. 15 Iowa and No. 16 USC lost in Big Ten play.

Did we expect Texas Tech to go on the road and lose to unranked Cincinnati?

No, but we also didn’t think the Red Raiders would look so lethargic in the process behind their expensive roster that is partially funded by mega-booster Cody Campbell.

The fact is that there is so much parity across college football right now that nothing should come as a surprise any longer, at least not during the 2026 season.

Whether it's Oregon losing its third game of the year, with a disaster of a performance against Illinois, or Michigan taking Indiana to overtime in the 'Big House', there is a weird vibe around the sport currently.

Who in the world are the best teams in college football?

What in the world is in the water around the Texas football facility?

One minute it's Arch Manning putting on a show for college football fans, and then it's the Longhorns going cold in the second half that has us all wondering why there is this tale of two halves with this Steve Sarkisian offense.

What we witnessed on Saturday night in Austin was essentially just another night in the SEC.

A back-and-forth slugfest between two teams that are capable of making a college football playoff run if everything is clicking. Somebody had to lose, and we still have plenty of questions lingering around both teams coming out of this one.

DID WE CREATE A MONSTER? ARCH MANNING'S 'AW SHUCKS' PERSONA IS GONE

Trinidad Chambliss is still that dude, as he proved in the second half of this matchup, and Arch Manning is still trying to figure out how to play consistent football for four quarters.

Each team is still in the running for the SEC title game, while every conference team besides Georgia and Kentucky has two losses.

And yes, that list now includes Tennessee after a fourth quarter frenzy by South Carolina.

I think Tennessee fans are still trying to figure out how they lost that football game, or putting some of the blame on the officiating (which i'd understand).

But, when the Vols couldn’t get out of their own way, South Carolina quarterback LaNorris Sellers and defensive end Dylan Stewart kicked the door down.

Another one of those hangovers, right? Maybe, but after a dominating performance against Alabama last week, one would’ve expected a better outing from the No. 11 ranked team in the country during the most important times of the game.

But, it was the Gamecocks who reeked havoc on the Vols once again at home, with head coach Shane Beamer even taking shots at those floating out conspiracy theories about the win over Tennessee in 2022 that was absorbed in talk of his team using signals stolen by Connor Stallions to win that game.

Yea, it got pretty weird on Saturday night in Columbia. But the only certain thing in the SEC is that nothing is for certain.

If the Red Raiders are expecting to still have a shot at making the college football playoff after losing on the road to Cincinnati, you can thank BYU for that glimmer of hope.

Judging by what we all witnessed, this Texas Tech team is obviously not in the same stratosphere as the 2025 roster, with Will Hammond struggling to complete passes against the Bearcats defense.

TEXAS TECH'S $30 MILLION ROSTER RUNS INTO A BUZZSAW AS CINCINNATI DELIVERS SORSBY REVENGE IN TOP-10 UPSET

item.title: Fugitive mom wanted in daughter’s Arizona murder used cartels to hide for years before capture in Mexico: feds
item.description: Anna Marlene Somoza's cartel connections helped her evade U.S. Marshals for over 12 years as a fugitive in Mexico after her daughter's 1997 death.
item.content:encoded:
Nearly 30 years after the death of her 3-year-old daughter, a mother has been arrested in Mexico by U.S. law enforcement officers on first-degree murder charges.

Anna Marlene Somoza, 60, was arrested by the U.S. Marshals Service after more than 12 years as a fugitive in Mexico. Her close connections to cartels allowed her to avoid apprehension, authorities said.

Somoza will be extradited to the United States to face charges for allegedly murdering her daughter, Crystal Reyes, according to the U.S. Marshals Service.

MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING PARTNER ARRESTED IN MEXICO NEARLY TWO YEARS AFTER FLEEING WITH THEIR TWO CHILDREN

Before her death, Reyes was subjected to severe abuse, torture and starvation, the agency said.

Confined to a small dog kennel, Reyes was bound by her hands and feet, gagged and left for weeks at a time. On Jan. 30, 1997, Reyes was bound, suffocated with a towel taped to her face, and left to die inside a sealed cardboard box, the agency said.

DNA TECHNOLOGY LEADS TO ARREST IN 1988 KILLING OF ORLANDO WOMAN AFTER NEARLY FOUR DECADES

Authorities began investigating after human bone fragments were found in a deserted area of Arizona by a hunter in November 1998. Almost two decades passed.

Then in August 2014, forensic DNA analysis identified the fragments of bone as remains of Reyes.

FORENSIC GENEALOGY UNMASKS COLD CASE SUSPECT AS STRANGLER, SEXUAL PREDATOR DECADES LATER: OFFICIALS

Detectives interviewed the child’s biological father and confirmed her identity using his DNA. Then, they said, they had sufficient grounds to charge Somoza and Avelino Tamala, her boyfriend at the time of Reyes’ death, with first-degree murder in December 2014.

Tamala was found guilty of Crystal’s murder in 2016. He was sentenced to life in prison.

DRUG CARTEL KINGPIN AMONG TARGETS IN SWEEPING TRUMP CRACKDOWN ON ALLEGED MEXICAN CORRUPTION NETWORK

But Somoza had been deported years earlier.

Somoza had an extensive criminal history before being charged in her daughter’s death. She had been connected to a major transnational drug trafficking network active along the southern Arizona border throughout the 1980s and 1990s.

After her 1993 arrest for the sale and transportation of marijuana, she agreed to act as a confidential informant for an Arizona law enforcement agency.

Through that, she met Tamala, a narcotics detective, and began "an improper romantic relationship," according to the U.S. Marshals Service.

SAN JOSE GIRL, 8, DIES AFTER LIVING IN COCKROACH-INFESTED HOME AS MOTHER, STEPFATHER FACE CHARGES

Not long after Reyes’ birth in Mexico in 1993, the mother and daughter began living with Tamala in Arizona, according to the agency. Tamala was not the father of Reyes.

The abuse Reyes endured likely wasn’t caught because she wasn’t attending school, said Stacy Vaughan, vice president of growth and prevention at Childhelp, a child abuse prevention organization.

"The majority of reports come from the education system in our country, from teachers, counselors, schools," Vaughan told Fox News Digital.

But a case like this may be prevented with the modern legislation in the United States, she said.

"In the past 20 years, many states have passed laws not only mandating that professionals report any suspected abuse, but…every adult over the age of 18 is considered a mandated reporter."

In 1999, the year after Reyes’ remains were found, Somoza and Tamala were arrested on drug- and weapon-related charges.

Somoza served eight years in federal prison and was deported in 2008.

After the child’s remains were connected to her as the mother in 2014, investigators from five state and federal agencies began to search for her.

She’d "taken deliberate and extensive measures to evade detection by law enforcement while remaining at large," according to a statement from the U.S. Marshals Service.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

In October 2022, authorities obtained an arrest warrant that would allow them to extradite her back to the United States. But they still needed to find her.

In 2026, the search for Somoza was designated a major case, "dedicating additional manpower and resources to the investigation," according to the U.S. Marshals Service.

In early September, the agency learned that Somoza was "actively evading detection" in Cuernavaca, Mexico, the agency said.

On Oct. 18, Mexican law enforcement officers caught her in Xochitepec, Mexico.

The U.S. Marshals Service now will work with the Mexican government to extradite Somoza to the United States, Russell Lorfing, a former federal prosecutor, told Fox News Digital.

They have "diplomatic assurances," Lorfing said. "But she will physically be handed over, and U.S. marshals will have to fly to Mexico. Or they'll arrange a coordinated kind of border handover."

The extradition process usually takes 14 days when it’s within the United States, Lorfing said. But international operations can take months. And they can stretch into years, if the defendant challenges the charges.
