item.title: ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ star Sarah Drew met husband leading worship at Christian youth camp
item.description: Sarah Drew reveals how meeting husband Pete Lanfer at a Christian youth camp nearly 30 years ago gave her a grounding force against Hollywood's chaos.
item.content:encoded:
"Grey's Anatomy" star Sarah Drew found lasting love long before she found Hollywood fame.

Drew opened up about meeting her husband while leading worship at a Christian youth camp nearly three decades ago. The actress, who has been married to Peter Lanfer for 24 years, credited their shared faith and strong partnership with helping her navigate the highs and lows of Hollywood. Drew and Lanfer married in 2002 and have two children.

"He's been my steady rock really and safe haven – since way before I had any success in this industry," Drew told Fox News Digital while promoting her upcoming movie, "Jimmy."

‘CHARLIE’S ANGELS’ STAR JACLYN SMITH LIVED APART FROM HER HUSBAND FOR 17 YEARS DURING THEIR 35-YEAR LOVE STORY

"And we have been real partners in parenting and in being humans in this world together," she added. "And I think anytime one of us is feeling shaky, the other one is always able to provide a safe harbor and some real like rock-solid strength for the other. So, I do think probably he's my greatest grounding force."

Drew described the entertainment industry as an unpredictable business that can celebrate an actor one moment and discard that person the next, explaining why she refuses to let Hollywood determine her self-worth.

"I think that it's very easy for Hollywood to tell you who you are. And what I mean by that is, they love you one second, they've forgotten you the next. You're gorgeous one second. They're tearing you to pieces the next. You're working all the time one second, all of a sudden, you're not working anymore, and you don't know what's going on. You never know when you're gonna work again. There is no stability anywhere."

Drew said the industry's constant uncertainty makes it difficult for actors to find a sense of stability in their careers.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"There is no place to be grounded in Hollywood. It just doesn't exist," she explained. "We are players to the whims of whoever is making the thing at the certain time and whoever's decided who's interesting or not, and I can't do anything about that."

"If I were not sure that my identity was firmly rooted first as a child of God, whose total identity is so much bigger than just who I am as an actress, if I wasn't rooted in that truth — and I know that truth to my cellular level and in my bones — I could so easily get caught up in the highs and think I'm God's gift to the Earth and then fall so miserably into I am absolutely worthless based on how Hollywood has decided to value me at any given time," she added.

Drew said her faith has helped her maintain a strong sense of identity beyond her career, reminding her that being a child of God, a wife, a mother and a friend matters more than her success as an actress.

Drew stars in "Jimmy," a biographical drama scheduled for nationwide theatrical release Nov. 6. The film follows actor James Stewart's military service, his struggles upon returning to Hollywood and his eventual comeback in the 1946 Christmas classic "It's a Wonderful Life," directed by Frank Capra.

Drew stars as Hedda Hopper, one of Hollywood's most influential and feared gossip columnists.

"18 months before we started shooting, Aaron Burns …reached out to me and told me that he'd gotten the rights and had a script for this movie, ‘Jimmy,’ that he was gonna make about this incredibly important time in Jimmy's life. And I've always been a huge fan of Jimmy Stewart," she said.

Drew said Burns told her he wanted her to play Hedda Hopper, but she didn't know much about the gossip columnist. Burns told her about "this formidable and complicated person." Drew said she doesn't "generally get the opportunity to play roles like this, so I said yes before I got off the phone, before I read the script."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

The "Supernatural" star's Christian faith has also influenced her decision to turn down acting opportunities. While Drew isn't opposed to exploring difficult subjects onscreen, she said she has rejected projects that she believed lacked a meaningful message.

"I have turned down jobs because I'm like, I don't know what we're supposed to walk away from this feeling," Drew explained. "I don't see any hope. I only see cynicism. Then I'm not interested."

Drew said she has always been drawn to stories that offer something meaningful rather than leaving audiences feeling hopeless.

"I just don't understand choosing something that is only going to make people feel darker or more devastated or more hopeless, like those kinds of things," she said. "And I think that that does very much stem from my faith and from my sense of the story that sort of bubbles through my life and has all through my upbringing. And through my adult life and as a parent and as a friend and all of these things, is that I want there to be hope associated with everything that I touch or am a part of – something that you can really like look toward as a beacon of goodness in some ways."

That philosophy also plays a central role in how Drew evaluates potential projects, a process she said often involves conversations with her husband. Rather than focusing on the prestige or financial rewards of a project, Drew said the couple first considers whether the story is one she wants to tell.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"It almost never is about what I might get paid, how fancy the project is, what network it's going to be on," she explained. "Those things are absolutely secondary to the first question, which is, 'Do you want to tell the story? Is this story that you think is going to resonate with people?'"

"I find that the stories that I'm drawn to are the ones that help people feel less alone and where someone can see themselves in a story," Drew said. "They can pick a redemption arc or a restoration arc and feel a little less alone. And they might laugh and cry and think on their way through the story of it, but at the end of it, they're like, 'Me too. I've also been through something like that. I know what that feeling is, and I feel a little less burdened and a little less alone because I have this opportunity to have this cathartic experience in a way that made me feel seen.'"

item.title: Socialism's growing appeal meets an awkward reality check on college campus
item.description: University of Michigan students offered over a dozen different definitions of socialism, reflecting a national confusion highlighted by Gallup polling.
item.content:encoded:
ANN ARBOR, Mich. — Socialism is gaining popularity among young Americans, but Fox News Digital found strikingly different understandings of the ideology among college students, some of whom acknowledged that their generation may not fully grasp what they're embracing.

A recent Fox News poll found that 48% of Americans ages 18 to 34 viewed socialism favorably, compared with 32% of Americans overall. When Fox News Digital asked more than a dozen University of Michigan students to define socialism, their answers ranged from government-funded safety nets and affordable health care to collective ownership of industry.

"If the definition was more widely known, people would support it less honestly," one student, Ahnika, told Fox News Digital.

Other students acknowledged the confusion, while at least a dozen declined to be interviewed on camera because they said they did not know enough about socialism to give an informed answer.

THE NUMBERS DON’T LIE. YOUNG AMERICANS ARE FALLING IN LOVE … WITH SOCIALISM

"Absolutely. I feel like many people don't really understand, I feel, the full grasp or scope of what socialism really means," a student named Owen told Fox News Digital. "I think they kind of have a more idealistic image of it."

The divide over what socialism actually means comes as the ideology becomes an increasingly prominent issue in American politics, including Michigan's closely watched Senate contest, where Republicans have sought to tie Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed to socialism – despite his rejection of the label.

Socialism? It's a safety net

Some of the students interviewed used the word socialism as a way to describe a government that spends more money on subsidizing healthcare, housing or other basic necessities.

"It's an economic system in which the resources of the government … are allocated into public services such as housing, affordable housing, food like food banks, education, things like that," James, one student, told Fox News Digital.

"Socialism to me is a concept in politics where everybody gets a little bit of everything. Everybody benefits and everybody is really taken care of. Kind of that social net that you see in other types of politics," Kayla, another student, said.

"It's a political system where less social goods are delivered by the market than in capitalism," said her fellow student, Sam.

Republicans and centrist Democrats have both raised concerns about the rising tide of socialism, while young people turn to it as a solution to the cost of living.

"Does the socialism thing scare me? Yes. Is it the wrong solution? Yes," Vice President JD Vance said in a July interview. "But one thing I try to persuade my fellow Republicans of is socialism is the alternative if we don’t have a pathway to give people a sense that the system is not rigged and that the American dream is attainable."

While the precise definition of socialism is debated by economists and philosophers, the ideology generally calls for replacing private ownership of major productive assets with some form of public, collective or worker ownership, though socialists differ sharply over whether that control should be exercised through the government, workers themselves or other institutions.

Modern socialism emerged as a major political and economic movement in 19th-century Europe, fueled by concerns over wealth inequality, industrial working conditions and the concentration of economic power in private hands.

A fair number of the students who spoke with Fox News Digital had understandings of socialism more in line with this traditional definition.

EL-SAYED REVEALS HE WOULD GO ‘STEP FURTHER’ THAN SANDERS ON SOCIALIST PLAN FOR MAJOR US INDUSTRY

Or is it government control?

"It's an economic system where certain aspects [of the economy] are controlled by the government such as health care, possibly housing, agriculture, general necessities," Owen said. "It's distinct from communism in that the government does not have free rein over every aspect of the market, but it's not the same as capitalism where the free market determines everything."

How far government control should extend has long divided socialists. Some advocate government ownership of nearly all major industries, while others favor worker-owned businesses amid a mix of public and private enterprise.

"I guess I would define it as an economic system where resources are shared in a more, in a somewhat equitable sense, and there's some level of, you know, public control of that," Zack, also a student at the university, told Fox News Digital. "It’s not really any more specific than that, socialism is a broad term, you know?"

While some young Americans associate socialism with government control of private businesses, an idea that has long faced resistance in American politics, the ideology has gained support among younger voters, even as they differ over what it would mean in practice. The Democratic Socialists of America, which advocates replacing capitalism with a more collectively controlled economy, has seen its ranks swell with members and notched a series of electoral victories during the second Trump administration.

"I'd say I define socialism by the government taking collective ownership of companies’ production and distribution of goods," student Ahnika told Fox News Digital.

"As far as I’m aware, it’s about like workers and members of society owning the product … as opposed to capitalism where you make the product, if you work on an assembly line, the product goes to your manager or whoever runs the factory and then they make most of the profit off of your work," Noah, also a student, told Fox News Digital.

Maybe it's Canada?

Others defined socialism in relation to countries or politicians.

"Mostly I think of Canada when I think of socialism," Samantha, another student, told Fox News Digital. Elyse, her peer, said that New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani comes to mind when thinking of a definition for socialism.

LIBERAL-CITY RESIDENT HESITATES WHEN PRESSED ON BELIEFS: 'I HADN'T REALLY THOUGHT ABOUT SOCIALISM THAT WAY'

The University of Michigan’s student body isn’t alone in its division over the definition of socialism.

Gallup found in 2018 that 23% of Americans thought the word meant "equality, including equal rights, standing or distribution," while 10% defined it as "provision of benefits and services, such as health care," 6% said it was "communism or a modified version of it" and further 6% understood it to be "being social or getting along with others."

Roughly a quarter of respondents had no opinion on the definition of socialism, and just 17% described it as "government ownership or control of businesses and the economy," the definition typically favored by economists.

Michigan, where many of the students interviewed vote, could easily decide control of Congress following November’s midterm elections. Socialism is a major issue in the race, with Republicans attempting to portray Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed as a socialist — a label he rejects despite a long-running association with the Democratic Socialists of America.

At least a dozen students told Fox News Digital that they were not comfortable filming an interview because they did not feel they knew enough about socialism to give an informed response, further highlighting the degree of confusion surrounding the term among young people.

LIBERAL HOT SPOT RESIDENTS CAN’T AGREE ON WHAT SOCIALISM MEANS AS FAR-LEFT MOVEMENTS GAINS STEAM

While the students couldn’t agree on what socialism meant, they did agree that their peers were confused.

"Yeah, I mean there's sort of a general idea of an equitable distribution of resources, but other than that, in terms of how it should be done, um like what it actually looks like, how power is distributed, there's a lot of open questions there," said Zach.

"Yeah, absolutely. There's a huge misconception about socialism, even capitalism as well," a student named Jeff told Fox News Digital. "So I think these terms in the broader space of political thought are probably allegories depending on your political orientation for good or bad … that's probably the most ubiquitous use of that term. ‘Socialism bad, capitalism good,’ or vice versa if you're a progressive."

THE MEDICARE FOR ALL TRADE-OFFS SOCIALISTS AREN'T TALKING ABOUT, ACCORDING TO EXPERTS

Other students felt their peers were too quick to define socialism in relation to other political systems.

"I would say some people would compare socialism to communism as being practically identical, whereas others would just understand it as having a stronger social safety net like in like Nordic countries," Sam said, noting that he doesn’t feel there is a right or wrong definition for the word.

"Yeah, I feel like a lot of people don't really understand what socialism is," Tommy, another student, said. "I feel like they think that sometimes it's communism and they conflate the two. So I feel like people need to educate themselves on what the concept actually is."

One student felt that, if more people understood socialism to imply government ownership of industry, the system would be significantly less popular.

"I honestly think there’s a bit of confusion … If the definition was more widely known, people would support it less honestly," Ahnika said. "Rather than having a good understanding of what socialism is, people often try to antagonize the opposite end of the spectrum, which is private ownership."

Not everyone felt that the ambiguity surrounding the term was necessarily a bad thing, however.

"I think having complex definitions of things only encourages conversation and when those conversations can be productive and when we approach them in a productive way I think we only uh strengthen what can be the collective definition of stuff like socialism," Elyse told Fox News Digital.

item.title: ENES KANTER FREEDOM: The WNBA says I'm a man. So why is it still afraid to say who is a woman?
item.description: The WNBA has made one thing clear: it is convinced that I am a man. The question now is whether Commissioner Engelbert and the WNBA are willing to tell America what makes someone a woman.
item.content:encoded:
Ladies and gentlemen, we finally have an answer from the WNBA.

Sort of.

After months of questions about who is eligible to compete in women's professional basketball, WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert has declared in an official letter that I am not eligible to play in the league.

WNBA TELLS CONGRESS THAT ENES KANTER FREEDOM, ROYCE WHITE ARE ‘BOTH MEN’ IN ELIGIBILITY DISPUTE

Why? Because Cuckoo Cathy identified me as a man. I was as shocked as you probably are to learn that a league that can't define what a woman is can so confidently identify a man.

But apparently, telling me I can't play wasn't enough. Now, the WNBA doesn't even want me in the stands as a paying customer.

On Wednesday night, I traveled to Atlanta to attend Game 3 of the WNBA Finals. I purchased premium courtside tickets, just like any other basketball fan. But when I arrived, I was informed that I would not be allowed to sit in the seats I purchased.

Instead, they decided I would have to watch the game from a private suite and enter through a private entrance, supposedly for my safety.

ENES KANTER FREEDOM GOES SCORCHED EARTH ON LEBRON JAMES, NBA WITH NEW REVELATIONS AFTER WNBA FINALS INCIDENT

I appreciate the concern for my safety. But I have spent years speaking out against authoritarian regimes that have threatened my life and my family. I am certainly not going to hide in a luxury suite because my presence makes someone uncomfortable.

I wanted to sit in the seats I paid for, watch the game, and continue standing up for women in sports. But when I refused to be moved out of sight, security denied me entry. I was escorted away from the arena.

For the second time, I was prevented from attending a WNBA game while speaking up for women. The WNBA is apparently more comfortable removing me from its arena than answering the questions I am asking.

And those questions begin with Commissioner Engelbert's response to Congressman Marlin Stutzman of Indiana. In her letter, she wrote, "only women are eligible to play in the WNBA and the individuals you cite in your letter are both men."

Notice what she did not say.

ENES FREEDOM LEAVES WNBA FINALS AFTER SPARRING WITH POLICE OVER SEATING CHANGE AMID SECURITY CONCERNS

She did not say that biological males are categorically ineligible to compete in the WNBA. She did not establish a biological standard for eligibility. She simply declared that I am a man and therefore cannot play.

Who gave Commissioner Engelbert the authority to determine my identity? What standards did she use to make that determination? And if she can so confidently identify me as a man, why can't the WNBA apply that same clarity to the question of who qualifies as a woman?

You cannot have it both ways.

The WNBA has reportedly assembled a task force to examine its eligibility policies. Yet we still have no publicly available, definitive policy establishing whether biological males who identify as women can compete in the league.

A task force. Meetings. Discussions. And still no clear answer to one of the most basic questions a women's sports league should be able to answer.

The women who have spent their entire lives training to compete at the highest level of their sport deserve to know that the rules protecting their opportunities will be applied fairly and consistently. And before that can happen, the rules must be clear.

WNBA HAS 'NO IDEA WHAT THEY'RE ABOUT TO FACE,' ENES KANTER FREEDOM SAYS AS LEAGUE TAKES ON TRANS ATHLETE ISSUE

That is why I am pursuing the opportunity to compete under the WNBA's rules. I have played professional basketball at the highest level, and I am prepared to pursue a place on a team. If the league believes I am ineligible, it should be able to identify the specific, consistently applied standard that disqualifies me.

Instead, the WNBA has created a contradiction.

The league knows I should not compete against women. It is willing to say so publicly. Yet it has not clearly explained whether the same biological considerations would disqualify another male athlete who identifies as a woman.

Is the league afraid of offending activists? Is it more concerned about political backlash than protecting its own athletes? Or does it simply want to leave the door open for exceptions while keeping someone like me out because I am willing to challenge its reasoning?

WNBA COMMISSIONER CATHY ENGELBERT BLAMES THE WRONG PEOPLE FOR ‘SOWING DIVISIVENESS’ IN TRANSGENDER DEBATE

I cannot tell you what is happening behind closed doors. But I can tell you what the public has been given.

A task force that has produced no clear public standard. A commissioner who can declare who is a man without explaining how she reaches that conclusion. And now, a league that would rather move a vocal fan out of public view than allow him to sit in the seats he purchased.

But this fight is about something much bigger than my eligibility or where I sit at a basketball game. It is about freedom. It is about fairness. And it is about the right to have your voice heard, especially when those in power would prefer your silence.

ROYCE WHITE EXPLORING LEGAL AVENUES AFTER WNBA TELLS CONGRESS HE IS INELIGIBLE TO PLAY

I know what it means to live under a government that punishes people for speaking their minds. I know what it means to have your freedom threatened because you refuse to remain silent. My criticism of authoritarianism has come at a tremendous personal cost, including separation from my family.

That is why, when I earned my American citizenship, I changed my last name to Freedom. That was not a publicity stunt. It was a declaration of gratitude, conviction and pride in my country. The fight to preserve freedom became part of my identity.

I believe every woman who steps onto a basketball court deserves the opportunity to compete fairly. I believe female athletes deserve to have their concerns heard, even when their opinions are unpopular. And I believe no athlete should feel pressured to sacrifice her convictions to protect her career.

Those are freedoms worth defending.

REPUBLICAN LAWMAKER BELIEVES THE WNBA SHOULD ADOPT THE OLYMPIC STANDARD FOR WOMEN’S SPORTS

Meanwhile, as this debate unfolds, players from the Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream have been running off the court before the national anthem, returning shortly after it concludes.

I understand that Americans have the freedom to protest. That is one of the things that makes this country extraordinary. But it brings us back to the distinction between having a right and being right.

America is not perfect, and it never has been. But this is also a nation where women have fought for and won opportunities that generations before them could scarcely imagine, including the opportunity to become professional athletes, compete on a national stage, and build careers playing the sport they love.

When I see athletes walk away from the American flag and an anthem that honors the costly battles fought for our freedom, I see an opportunity being missed. Those freedoms made their opportunities possible, and those opportunities deserve respect and protection.

There is a painful irony in watching players leave the court rather than stand for our anthem while the league responsible for protecting their competition seems equally determined to avoid taking a stand on fairness.

WNBA ANTHEM CONTROVERSY SPARKS CALLS TO BAR PLAYERS WHO DON'T STAND FROM TEAM USA'S OLYMPIC ROSTER

And now, when I show up to ask questions and stand up for those principles, the league wants me out of sight, too.

Freedom requires courage. So does fairness. Both demand that we defend principles even when doing so makes people uncomfortable. It requires us to stay in the arena and confront difficult questions about what is true and just rather than running away because we don't like the fight.

I have spent much of my life fighting for people whose voices powerful institutions would rather silence. I am not going to stop now simply because the institution in question happens to be a professional basketball league.

I am grateful to Congressman Stutzman for demanding answers, and I am glad Commissioner Engelbert finally responded. But her letter raises more questions than it answers.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

If I am ineligible because she says I am a man, then say plainly whether all biological males are ineligible for the same reason. If biological sex is not the determining factor, explain what is. And if the WNBA believes women's sports deserve protection, establish a clear, consistent policy that actually protects them.

The WNBA can deny me a spot on the court. It can deny me the seats I purchased. It can even escort me out of the arena. Again. But it cannot make me stop asking questions. And it cannot make me stop fighting for the women whose opportunities, voices, and freedoms deserve to be protected.

I did not change my last name to Freedom because I wanted to avoid uncomfortable fights. I changed it because I know how precious freedom is and how easily it can be lost when people are afraid to defend what they know is right.

item.title: Jessie James Decker shares 'secret sauce' behind family's food, faith, traditions
item.description: Country singer Jessie James Decker reveals her family's game day food traditions, favorite recipes and how Catholic faith shapes life around the dinner table.
item.content:encoded:
Country singer Jessie James Decker has spent years balancing music and business with raising a growing family, but some of her favorite moments happen around the dinner table.

Decker recently released "The Secret Sauce: A Family Cookbook Seasoned with Love," which she wrote with her mother, Karen Parker, and sister Sydney Rae Bass.

The cookbook draws on the family's Southern, Sicilian and Cajun roots, bringing together recipes and traditions passed down through generations and shared at family gatherings. It includes everything from weeknight meals and game-day dishes to holiday recipes and desserts.

CELEBRITY CHEF SAYS PEOPLE HAVE SOUTHERN FOOD ALL WRONG, SHARES WHAT HER FAMILY ATE

For Jessie James Decker, food is closely connected to both family and faith.

The singer and author told Fox News Digital that her Catholic faith has long played an important role in her family, something she credits her mother with passing down.

"Faith has always been a big part of my life and our lives," Jessie James Decker said.

She said her mother taught the family to turn to prayer during both difficult and joyful seasons of life.

CELEBRITY CHEF SAYS MILITARY LESSON IS KEY TO KEEPING FAMILIES TOGETHER

"You just have to trust in Him, because His plan is so much greater than you could ever imagine," Jessie James Decker said.

Those values also carry into life at home with her husband, former NFL wide receiver Eric Decker, and their four children.

One of the family's traditions is sitting down together for dinner, with electronics put away, so everyone has a chance to catch up.

"It's not even that hard to get rid of the electronics when it's time for dinner because we want to talk to each other," Jessie James Decker said.

"We just get so excited to have that time with each other, to be present, to ask about each other's day."

Jessie James Decker said she often goes around the table and asks each child a question, sometimes something silly, to get everyone talking.

"Those memories and moments with my family around the dinner table are just my favorite," she said.

Cooking itself has become another way Jessie James Decker connects with her children.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

She described making food as one of her strongest "love languages," saying she takes pride in preparing meals for her family and watching her children enjoy them.

"I just get such pride, such joy from making food to nourish their bodies and fill their tummies," Jessie James Decker said.

Her children have already developed their own favorites from her kitchen.

Daughter Vivi loves seafood gumbo, while sons Eric and Forrest enjoy her pasta dishes. Her youngest, Denver, is also a gumbo fan, Jessie James Decker said.

Eric Decker's favorite is her chicken pot pie, while steak, salads and balsamic green beans are among other dishes that make their way onto the family table.

Her husband's football background has also shaped some of their food traditions.

On game days, Jessie James Decker said she typically makes chili, barbecue meatballs and some type of dip, occasionally adding wings to the spread.

"Every game day we definitely get after it," she said.

That mix of family recipes, traditions and memories helped shape "The Secret Sauce," which Decker said is ultimately about more than what is being served.

"The secret sauce is just the love and joy that you put into cooking, and it's not just about the food," she said.

item.title: Why the under makes sense as the 5-0 Kansas City Chiefs visit the Seattle Seahawks
item.description: Patrick Mahomes and the 5-0 Kansas City Chiefs face Sam Darnold's struggling Seattle Seahawks on Sunday Night Football in a clash of recent champions.
item.content:encoded:
"Sunday Night Football" has been one of the best games of the week almost every week this season. The league reserves one of the best matchups of the week to put in that slot, and they’ve done that for us this week. One of the things I like most about this game is that we see two of the past three Super Bowl champions taking each other on as the Chiefs take on the Seahawks.

The Kansas City Chiefs had a disaster of a season last year, and honestly, I was one of the people who counted them out quite a bit this season. Last year they looked old, disjointed, disinterested, and overall bad. This season, the Chiefs have found a way to a 5-0 record, but their bye week has already passed, which makes me think they will lose some games late in the season. It gets harder to win as the games start piling up, and those later bye weeks help to heal injuries.

So far, though, the team looks great, and the offense seems back to normal after a down year last season.

Patrick Mahomes is back from an ACL tear suffered late last season. Mahomes has 1,309 passing yards, nine touchdowns, and three interceptions for the season. Their biggest addition was Kenneth Walker III, who is averaging about 6 yards per carry, and he has six touchdowns on the ground.

The dynamic of a tough running game keeps the defense guessing, and that’s really all the Chiefs need to be deadly. The passing defense hasn’t been elite this season, but the rushing defense has been very good.

The Seattle Seahawks have struggled a bit this season and are just 3-3 coming into the game. Sam Darnold looks like he is back to making bad decisions. He has 1,033 passing yards, seven touchdowns, and seven interceptions for the season. His most recent was against the Broncos last week, and he threw an interception in overtime, which, for all intents and purposes, gave Denver the victory.

This was the third loss in four weeks for Seattle. They do get a bit of an advantage because they played Thursday last week, so they have a bit of extra rest.

None of the losses for Seattle are bad. All three are by three points or fewer. Their running game has been almost non-existent this season, especially compared to last year. Jaxon Smith-Njigba is still one of the best in the league, and he has hauled in seven touchdowns this year. Still, the Seahawks can’t be that one-dimensional.

Their wins this year have been against a Patriots team that looked awful in Week 1 – with Drew Lock coming in for Darnold early in the game. Then they beat a Cardinals team that is mediocre, and the Charges who haven’t won at all.

WHY DEFENDING SUPER BOWL CHAMPION SEATTLE SEAHAWKS COULD STRUGGLE TO MATCH LAST SEASON'S 14-3 RECORD

The lone loss the Seahawks have taken at home this season was against the 49ers. I’m not believing that the Chiefs will go 17-0, but I do think the team will win this game. Their defense has been very good, but more importantly, the offense looks like it is back to being unique. Seattle has a strong rushing defense, but Walker is probably on a mission to show the Seahawks what they are missing.

Seattle has the best passing defense, so the under makes a ton of sense as well. I’ll put a half unit on the Chiefs to win and a half unit on the under.

item.title: Browns vs Titans NFL Week 7 betting preview favors Cleveland's defense on the moneyline
item.description: Cleveland Browns enter Week 7 at 4-2 with a stingy defense allowing just 20.3 points per game as they face the 1-5 Tennessee Titans on the moneyline.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL season is moving at a quick pace, and we have already reached Week 7. It has been a bit of a wild season already. Some teams that were struggling were picked to be great this season, and some teams that were picked to be bad are already exceeding expectations. The Chargers were expected to be strong this year, but they’ve been terrible. The Browns, on the other hand, have been surprisingly good, and they take on the Titans this afternoon.

The Cleveland Browns come into this game at 4-2 for the season, but both of their losses have come on the road this season. The first loss was to the Jaguars in the first game of the season, and the Browns looked like a complete disaster. They ran off three straight wins over the Buccaneers, Panthers, and Steelers.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Then they had to face the Jets and couldn’t get much going on offense. They lost that game 17-12, not scoring a touchdown. Last week, they won at the buzzer against the Ravens.

After trading away their best defensive player, the outlook for the season was a bit low, but their defense has been surprisingly good. They are only allowing 20.3 points per game to opponents. They are eighth in the league in passing defense. The running defense hasn’t been exactly good either. They have 112.3 rushing yards allowed per game to opponents, but the Titans aren’t a really good running team, so this might not be much of an issue. The bigger question is if Deshaun Watson can figure out the Titans' defense.

The Tennessee Titans are coming off their first victory of the season. This one was a disappointment for me because I had the Colts in the game, but they p----- away the game. The Titans are not a very good football team, but they do deserve credit for finding a way to get the game across the finish line. They took the lead, then instantly gave up the lead. On the ensuing possession, a pass interference call gave them great field position, and they took a field goal lead. They added another, and the Colts lost the game.

I may have phrased it wrong; the Colts lost it, but the Titans won the game. They started the season with a loss to the Jets. Then they lost to the Eagles, Giants, Ravens, and Texans.

Three of those five losses were by one score, though. Perhaps the goal for the Titans this year is how to figure out winning close games. I suppose either way, it should be viewed as a step in the correct direction. They don’t necessarily win games, but at least they aren’t getting blown out, and they are being competitive. Their defense is in the bottom half of the league in terms of running yards allowed, but the Browns don’t really have a great running game either. The passing defense is about middle of the pack.

However, I do think the Browns will win this game and we should take them on the moneyline at -130. They have the better defense, and I do think their offense will have just enough of an edge, but this might be sweaty.

item.title: Human vs. ChatGPT NFL Week 7 betting picks: Human clings to profit as AI claims third straight win
item.description: Human analyst is still profitable by just 0.09 units as he takes on ChatGPT with five more NFL bets, including a Titans upset and a shared Bengals pick.
item.content:encoded:
Apparently, the robot doesn't even have to make money to beat me anymore.

ChatGPT finished Week 6 at 2-2-1 and lost 0.16 units. I went 2-3 and lost 1.17 units. That's three straight weeks of GPT getting the better of me, although I'm not sure "congratulations on losing less money" is quite the victory speech it had in mind.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The good news? I'm still profitable this season. The bad news? My profit is now 0.09 units. Yes, there's still a plus sign in front of my total, and I intend to keep pointing that out until someone makes me stop. I'm 15-14-1 through six weeks, while GPT is 13-16-1 and down 4.03 units.

To make matters worse, the Chargers handed "Dan Z.'s plug your nose and hit place bet" pick its first loss of the season. That streak ends at four after Los Angeles managed six points against Kansas City. It's my own fault; and, I know I keep saying this, but this time I mean it: I am OFF the Chargers this season.

Anyway, we're back for Week 7. I'd like to get back to winning money before my entire season profit disappears into a rounding error.

Both of us get five selections from the same odds board, with a maximum price of -120. Odds were captured Saturday at 6 p.m. ET.

The stakes are adjusted so every winning bet produces one unit of profit. For example, -110 requires risking 1.10 units, while +110 requires 0.91 units. A push returns the stake and counts as zero units.

Before we get to the Week 7 picks, let’s review last week.

The Bears-Falcons under was looking great until Ben Johnson started resting defensive starters in the fourth quarter. Atlanta promptly scored a touchdown and converted the two-point attempt. Chicago put the starters back in, and the Falcons scored another touchdown and another two-point conversion anyway. All they had to do was stop one two-point conversion and we hit. Lame.

We don't need to talk about the Chargers or the Cowboys because they both stink. Those two are squarely on me (not every loss is my fault, you see).

The Raiders stayed within the number in Buffalo, and Washington salvaged my Monday night with a six-point loss to San Francisco. When you're celebrating two teams losing football games, you know you've had a productive week.

GPT went all-in on totals and got the full experience: two wins, two losses and a game that landed exactly on the number.

DAN: 15-14-1, +0.09 units

GPT: 13-16-1, -4.03 units

Dan Z.’s Plug Your Nose and Hit 'Place Bet' Bet of the Week: 4-1, +2.90 units

Cleveland Browns at Tennessee Titans, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET

Dan’s analysis:

This is the official "Dan Z.'s plug your nose and hit place bet" bet of the week. Because nothing says "I've learned from my mistakes" like following up a losing Chargers bet by taking the 1-5 Titans to win outright. But I don't think Cleveland is nearly as good as its 4-2 record suggests. Deshaun Watson has quietly been very bad, and the Browns keep escaping with late wins that cover up how poorly he's playing.

Tennessee, meanwhile, has been competitive in three of its five losses and finally got a win last week. There's more fight here than people think. I'm getting plus money at home against a team I'm not buying. So, yes, we're doing this again.

GPT’s analysis:

Cleveland’s 4-2 record looks better than an offense averaging just 17.7 points per game, so I understand backing the home underdog. The Browns have repeatedly needed late recoveries, which makes them difficult to trust as road favorites. My concern is Tennessee’s ability to capitalize: Cam Ward faces a strong Cleveland pass defense, and the Titans have struggled to sustain offense themselves. At +112, Tennessee needs to win roughly 47% of the time to justify the price.

I lean Cleveland -2, although neither side made my five.

Cincinnati Bengals at Baltimore Ravens, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET

Dan’s analysis:

Cincinnati needs to start establishing itself, and this is a pretty good opportunity. The Bengals are coming off a bye, Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins have had extra time to get healthy, and Lamar Jackson has officially been ruled out. There aren't many excuses left.

I think Cincinnati's improved defense should feast against a Baltimore offense that loses so much of what makes it dangerous without Lamar. On the other side, I'm trusting Joe Burrow and his receivers to take advantage. All I'm asking is for the Bengals to win by a field goal. They've certainly found ways to disappoint me before, but I'm going back.

GPT’s analysis:

We agree on this one. Cincinnati comes out of its bye without any injury game designations, while Baltimore will again start Tyler Huntley with Lamar Jackson ruled out. That gives the Bengals advantages in quarterback play, preparation and availability. My concern is Derrick Henry against Cincinnati’s uneven run defense, which gives Baltimore a way to stay competitive without asking Huntley to carry the offense. Still, Burrow is the quarterback I trust to produce the necessary scoring drives.

Getting Cincinnati below three is the deciding factor: a field-goal win covers. This was my top selection.

San Francisco 49ers at Atlanta Falcons, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET

Dan’s analysis:

The 49ers' injury report looks like a MASH unit. Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel are both out, and I don't see San Francisco deciding this is the week to start chucking the ball all over the field. I expect a lot of running, short passes and making Atlanta tackle people.

I also think that's the kind of game Kyle Shanahan wants here. Getting into a track meet against an offense featuring Bijan Robinson and Drake London doesn't seem like the best plan with this many guys missing. Drag the Falcons into a slugfest, keep the clock moving and make every possession take forever. It might not be particularly fun to watch, but I've never required my winning bets to be entertaining.

GPT’s analysis:

San Francisco’s receiver injuries and both teams’ rushing tendencies give your under a credible foundation. Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel are out, and Atlanta getting A.J. Terrell back could further restrict the 49ers’ passing opportunities. My concern is that San Francisco can still generate efficient offense through Christian McCaffrey and George Kittle, while Atlanta’s defense has allowed at least 30 points in consecutive games. Missing receivers do not necessarily mean the 49ers will struggle to score.

I understand the under, but Atlanta’s defensive vulnerability kept it outside my five.

New York Giants at Houston Texans, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET

Dan’s analysis:

This game screams UNDER, so of course we're going with the OVER.

Houston's defense has been exploitable this season and doesn't look like the unit we saw last year. J.J. McCarthy gives the Giants a little more juice, and I think he can help them put points on the board. Of course, he could also make a terrible decision that gives Houston a short field. For once, I'm in a position to appreciate either outcome.

The Texans have scored at least 26 points in three straight games, and adding Marvin Harrison Jr. gives defenses another receiver to worry about besides Nico Collins. I think Houston keeps scoring, and the Giants contribute enough to get us over a pretty low number.

NFL WEEK 6 SUNDAY TAKEAWAYS: GIANTS HAVE A NEW QB1, BILLS KEEP ROLLING AND SHANE STEICHEN IS ON THE HOT SEAT

GPT’s analysis:

The defensive injuries give your over a strong starting point. New York is missing Jevón Holland, Greg Newsome and Tremaine Edmunds, creating opportunities for C.J. Stroud. Houston is also without safeties Jalen Pitre and Reed Blankenship, giving the Giants a potential scoring route. My hesitation is J.J. McCarthy’s first Giants start: his late production against New Orleans came with the game already heavily tilted against New York. That does not establish that he can sustain touchdown drives against Houston’s pass rush.

The over has a case, but uncertainty about the Giants’ contribution kept it off my card.

Green Bay Packers at Detroit Lions, Sunday at 4:25 p.m. ET

Dan’s analysis:

I've been doubting the Packers, but at some point I have to stop arguing with a team that keeps winning. Beating my Cowboys pick last week certainly helped get my attention. I think Green Bay is the better team with the better coach, and I'm getting more than a field goal.

Going on the road in the division is tough, but I actually like this offense on turf. Matthew Golden and Christian Watson can fly, and playing indoors gives them a chance to show it. Plus, Josh Jacobs is back. This offense doesn't need a dominant running game. It just needs enough production to make defenses respect it, and Jacobs should give them that. Give me the points.

GPT’s analysis:

Getting more than a field goal with Jordan Love against a Detroit defense allowing 29.6 points per game is appealing. Christian Watson and Matthew Golden are available, giving Green Bay the receiving options to exploit that matchup. My concern is the other side of the ball: the Packers are missing linebackers Zaire Franklin and Edgerrin Cooper, creating a difficult assignment against Jahmyr Gibbs. Detroit also has the preparation advantage coming out of its bye.

This was one of the better sides I left out. The hook matters: a three-point Detroit win still cashes your ticket.

For full transparency, I used GPT-6.1 Sol and set the thinking effort to Ultra (highest available). Then, I fed it the OddsChecker board as it appeared Saturday at 6 p.m. ET and gave it the following prompt:

"Pick your five best bets for Week 7 based on the odds provided. No bet can be priced worse than -120. Review every spread, total and moneyline that falls within those parameters and determine whether it belongs among your five picks. Explain exactly why you’re selecting each of the five bets. Also explain exactly why you’re passing on the eligible bets you don’t select. Use at least 10 different sources for each game so you have a broad understanding of everything surrounding each game. Before delivering the results, do a fact-check and ensure that everything is correct."

Pittsburgh Steelers vs. New Orleans Saints, Sunday at 9:30 a.m. ET in Paris

GPT’s analysis:

Pittsburgh ranks second in rushing DVOA, while New Orleans ranks last in rush-defense DVOA. That gives Jaylen Warren a favorable matchup and reduces the need for Aaron Rodgers to force throws downfield. T.J. Watt is available to challenge Tyler Shough. Pittsburgh’s late arrival in Paris and injuries elsewhere are concerns, but the rushing and defensive advantages outweigh them at this number.

I prefer laying three to betting the total. A field-goal Pittsburgh win returns the stake.

GPT’s projected score: Steelers 24, Saints 20

Dan’s analysis:

The Saints have burned me enough this season that I understand the appeal of betting against them. Unfortunately, I still can't quite quit Tyler Shough and this offense. Apparently, I need to lose more money before I learn that lesson. I'm not backing New Orleans this week, but I'm not ready to lay points against them, either. I'll watch this one without a financial reason to be annoyed.

Cincinnati Bengals at Baltimore Ravens, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET

GPT’s analysis:

Cincinnati comes out of its bye without any injury game designations, while Baltimore will again start Tyler Huntley with Lamar Jackson ruled out. Joe Burrow gives the Bengals the quarterback advantage, and the extra preparation strengthens their case. Derrick Henry against Cincinnati’s uneven run defense is the biggest concern, especially if Baltimore can control possession and keep Burrow off the field. Still, Cincinnati has the healthier roster and more dependable passing offense.

The number makes this my top selection: a three-point Bengals victory covers.

GPT’s projected score: Bengals 27, Ravens 20

Dan’s analysis:

Obviously, we're together on this one. Cincinnati is coming off a bye, Lamar is out, and we only need the Bengals to win by a field goal. I like the setup for all the reasons I already laid out. If Cincinnati finds a way to screw this up, at least the robot and I can complain about it together next week.

Indianapolis Colts at Minnesota Vikings, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET

GPT’s analysis:

Minnesota allows just 12.8 points per game, and its pressure-heavy defense presents a difficult assignment for Daniel Jones without Tyler Warren. Indianapolis also loses Sauce Gardner, weakening its coverage as Minnesota gets Jordan Addison and T.J. Hockenson back. The Vikings’ own offensive inefficiency is the biggest concern, while Jonathan Taylor gives Indianapolis a way to stay competitive. However, Minnesota’s defensive advantage, extra preparation and improving availability make this a favorable matchup.

At -105, I’m comfortable laying less than a touchdown. A seven-point win covers.

GPT’s projected score: Vikings 24, Colts 16

Dan’s analysis:

I don't know why, but I have a sneaky feeling the Colts are going to show up on Sunday. Probably not enough to win, but enough to make laying nearly a touchdown uncomfortable. Indianapolis just missed my card. GPT has plenty of reasonable arguments here, and I have a feeling. We'll see how that works out.

Denver Broncos at Arizona Cardinals, Sunday at 4:05 p.m. ET

GPT’s analysis:

Denver and Arizona average just 4.4 and 4.6 yards per play, respectively, and neither offense consistently creates explosive gains. Arizona is also without Jeremiyah Love. The biggest concerns are Arizona’s vulnerable pass defense giving Bo Nix a breakthrough opportunity and Denver missing Talanoa Hufanga with Pat Surtain questionable. Still, both passing offenses have struggled enough that ordinary stalled possessions can keep this below the number.

I prefer the under to asking Denver’s limited offense to cover more than a field goal.

GPT’s projected score: Broncos 23, Cardinals 17

Dan’s analysis:

I looked at this under but ultimately passed. Arizona moved the ball against the Rams last week; it just kept settling for field goals. The Cardinals also got an unusually strong performance from a defense that has given up plenty of points this season, and I'm not ready to trust that happening again. Denver's offense isn't great, but it should be able to score against Arizona. I see enough ways for this to get over the number to stay away.

Kansas City Chiefs at Seattle Seahawks, Sunday at 8:20 p.m. ET

GPT’s analysis:

Kansas City leads the league at 6.7 offensive yards per play, while its defense can challenge a Seattle offense struggling to establish the run. That gives the Chiefs a credible path to keeping this close or winning outright. Seattle’s extra rest, home field and strong four-man pass rush are substantial concerns, particularly with Kansas City missing Rashee Rice and Jaylon Moore. Kansas City has also faced relatively weak defenses, which warrants caution when evaluating its offensive numbers.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

I prefer taking the full field goal to the moneyline, preserving a push if Seattle wins by three.

GPT’s projected score: Chiefs 23, Seahawks 20

Dan’s analysis:

If I had to pick a side, I'd take Seattle. The Seahawks should have a plan for Kenneth Walker III, and if they can stop him, I'm interested to see what Kansas City's offense looks like. I don't think it will look particularly good. It's not strong enough for me to put Seattle on my card, but I'd lean toward the Seahawks winning by more than a field goal.

OK, that's it for Week 7! I feel good about this card and I think I'm going to smoke GPT. If not, I might retire.

Just kidding.

No, seriously, I might.

Week 7 of the NFL has the first game kicking off at 9:30 a.m. ET and running for the remainder of the day. Betr is offering new users $200 in bonuses and sweat-free picks with promo code FOXNEWS for NFL Week 7.

There are plenty of great matchups today, but one worth playing takes place early in the day as the 49ers take on the Falcons. The best team in the NFL heads to Atlanta, looking to remain perfect. On the other side, the Falcons are looking to try and get closer to .500 after having a very different season. 

The San Francisco 49ers are 6-0 with one of the best offenses and defenses in football. It doesn’t look like they will slow down any time soon. Brock Purdy is playing like an MVP. George Kittle has been elite and looks like he is turning back the clock. Christian McCaffrey already has seven touchdowns on the ground and continues to chew up yardage as one of the most versatile backs in the league. Most of all, the team seems to be healthy, which is not something they could say in previous years. 

The Atlanta Falcons enter the game with a 2-4 record and inconsistent quarterback play at best. In their defense, Cooper Rush has been the starter a couple of times, and he didn’t play very well, so that put the Falcons behind the 8-ball, so to speak. Michael Penix Jr. has been good, for the most part, but last game he struggled to figure out the Bears' defense. Eventually, the team got there, but it was too little, too late for the Falcons. They dropped their second straight game and are now on the verge of losing three straight and really hindering their playoff chances.

Can the 49ers stay perfect for the season, or will the Falcons throw a wrench into their plans? Can Penix Jr. figure out one of the better defenses in the league, or will San Francisco stop the inconsistent Falcons?
